tldr: The authors propose DASH, a system that decouples a VLA model asynchronously into slow semantic understanding (VLM) and fast action generation (action head), maintaining a 20 Hz control rate without slowdown even when using massive models.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of DASH. Three processes—the environment process, the slow VLM server (System 2), and the fast action server (System 1)—communicate asynchronously via LCM. By removing the VLM from the control-critical path, scaling up the VLM model size causes no reduction in the control rate.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which embed large vision-language models (VLMs) into action generation, have drawn great attention as a key approach to general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, in closed-loop control on physical robots—especially for humanoid manipulation with high-degree-of-freedom hands—inference latency poses a fatal bottleneck. Scaling up models to improve generalization extends inference time. Because the real world continues to evolve while the robot computes its actions, executed actions are conditioned on increasingly stale observations. Consequently, synchronous pipelines face an inherent trade-off where scaling up the model reduces the control rate, causing jerky movements or task failures.

The authors recognized that this trade-off stems from running all processing synchronously, and that it can be resolved by separating the policy into a slow thinking system (System 2) and a fast reflexive system (System 1), akin to the human brain. To this end, they propose DASH (Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids). DASH runs the slow VLM responsible for semantic understanding and the fast flow-matching action head outputting action chunks as completely independent concurrent processes. As a result, the control rate is determined solely by the speed of the action head, achieving latency-agnostic scaling where control rates do not drop even with a massive VLM. Furthermore, to bridge the mismatch between stale semantics and fresh visual information caused by asynchronous execution, the action head incorporates its own fresh vision encoder, and desynchronized training simulates deployment time lags during training.

The authors evaluated DASH on a 50-task RoboTwin benchmark that strictly charges inference latency in simulated time, as well as on a physical bimanual humanoid with dexterous hands. When scaling the VLM backbone from 0.8B to 8B, the synchronous control rate plummeted from 9.7 Hz to 4.1 Hz, whereas DASH consistently held a 20 Hz rate across all sizes while outperforming synchronous models in success rate at every size. In real-robot language-instructed pick-and-place trials, DASH achieved an overwhelming success rate of 23/24 compared to 16/24 for the conventional synchronous baseline.
contributions: Built DASH, an asynchronous dual-system that removes the heavy VLM from the VLA control loop so that a fast action head alone determines the control rate.
Maintained a constant 20 Hz control rate regardless of VLM parameter size (0.8B to 8B), reconciling the generalization of large models with high-frequency reactivity.

Seamlessly fused stale semantic context with fresh visual cues using a dedicated fresh vision encoder in the action head and desynchronized training that simulates deployment latency distributions during training.
Proposed an adaptive temporal aggregator that smoothly stitches overlapping action chunks across varying per-inference latencies using fractional linear interpolation.

sections.heading: Why does making models larger make robot motions clumsy?
sections.summary: When deploying VLA models on physical robots, longer inference latencies cause predicted actions to be conditioned on stale observations. To overcome the trade-off where scaling models for better generalization degrades latency, the authors propose DASH, asynchronously decoupling the system into fast and slow components.
sections.details:
VLA models are becoming mainstream in general-purpose robotic manipulation, but the passage of real time impacts closed-loop physical control severely. Unlike evaluations on offline datasets, the physical world never pauses while the robot moves. If inference takes $L$ seconds, an action chunk computed from an observation at time 0 only arrives at time $L$, by which point the robot has already moved into subsequent states. This temporal mismatch does not appear in offline validation loss metrics, but on real hardware it manifests as motion delays, hesitations, and violent vibrations, which are catastrophic for humanoid dexterous manipulation requiring delicate contact.

This directly collides with VLA scaling laws. Increasing model size improves instruction following and generalization, but it also increases inference latency $L$. In short, researchers have been forced into a painful choice between intelligence and swift reactivity.

The authors argue that this problem is merely an artifact of synchronous execution. Biological organisms and physical robots are inherently asynchronous systems where sensory input, high-level cognition, and low-level motor control operate at their own distinct frequencies. DASH therefore decouples the architecture into a slow VLM (System 2) responsible for semantic understanding and a fast action head (System 1) responsible for high-frequency action generation. Taking the VLM off the control-critical path enables latency-agnostic scaling, where control rate is never sacrificed no matter how large the VLM grows. Moreover, because earlier steps in an action chunk are more reliable while later steps carry higher uncertainty, continuously updating with fresh chunks substantially boosts motion stability.

sections.heading: How does this differ from existing fast-slow robot control architectures?
sections.summary: While scaling VLAs and dual-system fast-slow architectures have been explored previously, most prior approaches remain synchronous or handle latency heuristically. DASH distinguishes itself by addressing the feature-level temporal mismatch caused by inference latency through an end-to-end asynchronous design across both learning and communication.
sections.details:
### II-A VLM Backbone Scaling and Adaptation
Early VLAs such as RT-2 showed that knowledge from web-scale pre-trained models could be transferred to robots, but their models were too large to reach real-time control rates. Consequently, recent methods like OpenVLA, $\pi_0$, and GR00T N1 keep backbones relatively compact (around 2B to 7B) or freeze parts of them to train action heads. Nevertheless, the VLM itself still sits inside the control loop in many of these designs, leaving the structural bottleneck where model size caps the control rate unchanged.

### II-B Fast-Slow Dual Systems
The concept of pairing a slow high-level system with a fast low-level system has been explored in prior works such as GR00T N1 and Helix. However, many still synchronize training and execution, leaving core challenges of asynchronous control unaddressed—such as how stale the slow system's output becomes before reaching the fast system, and how to reconcile overlapping action chunks under varying inference latencies.

### II-C Latency-Aware Robot Control
Existing techniques to counter inference latency include RTC, which interpolates running actions and new chunks at their boundary, and VLASH, which rolls states forward into the future before prediction. However, these methods geometrically compensate for delays in states or actions themselves; they do not directly resolve how to harmonize stale features (context) from a slow system with fresh observations in a fast decoupled dual-system.

sections.heading: How DASH works: Fusing cognition and reflexes running on independent clocks
sections.summary: DASH runs three processes—environment, VLM, and action head—fully asynchronously via LCM communication. The action head incorporates a ResNet looking at fresh images to fuse with stale semantics; robust control is achieved via desynchronized training that injects random temporal lags during training and an adaptive temporal aggregator that smoothly connects fractional offsets.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
In conventional synchronous VLAs, generating an action chunk of length $H$ from images, states, and instructions delays execution by the inference latency $L$ (execution latency $\delta_{\text{exec}} = L$). Increasing model size $N$ inflates $L$, leading to control failure. Decoupling them asynchronously minimizes execution latency $\delta_{\text{exec}}$ because it is determined solely by the action head's inference time. The cost, however, is a newly introduced context latency ($\delta_{\text{ctx}}$), meaning the VLM context $c_{t-\Delta t}$ received by the action head is stale by one slow cycle. DASH aims to minimize $\delta_{\text{exec}}$ independently of model size while acquiring robustness against $\delta_{\text{ctx}}$.

### III-B Decoupled Latency-Agnostic Architecture
DASH divides the entire system into three independent processes: the Environment, the VLM Server (System 2), and the Action Server (System 1). Inter-process communication uses LCM, a lightweight UDP-based protocol. The environment process continuously publishes fresh sensor data, and each server pulls only the latest message from its queue for inference. With lock-free latest-value semantics, processes never block waiting for each other to finish. The control frequency $f_{\text{ctrl}}$ depends solely on the action head throughput $f_{\text{action}}$, remaining completely independent of VLM size $N$.

### III-C Cross-Timescale Fusion and In-Head Vision Encoder
The VLM utilizes a pre-trained Qwen3-VL with completely frozen weights. The action head employs a 12-layer Flow-matching DiT (Diffusion Transformer) that generates actions via 4-step numerical integration. Hidden features are extracted from four layers located at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of the VLM backbone and injected into DiT layers via cross-attention. A crucial architectural design is equipping the action head with its own ResNet-152 vision encoder. While visual features from the frozen VLM are stale by the time they arrive, the action head feeds fresh visual tokens from its own ResNet running on its own clock, concatenating them with stale semantic features to enable rapid end-effector fine adjustments conditioned on the latest scene state.

### III-D Desynchronized Training for Train-Test Consistency
During deployment, the policy always receives a combination of stale VLM context and fresh end-effector observations. If trained on data sampled at identical timestamps ($\Delta t = 0$), the model encounters an out-of-distribution input at inference and degrades. To resolve this, the authors introduce Desynchronized Training, where only the input frame to the VLM is sampled with a random backward time lag $\Delta$ (up to the maximum frame lag observed on real hardware). Without adding latency flags or specialized tokens, shifting only the input data timing teaches the model to naturally harmonize coarse stale context with fresh visual feedback.

### III-E Adaptive Temporal Aggregator for Asynchronous Inference
Action chunks emitted in succession by the action head overlap in time, requiring averaging for smoothness. In asynchronous inference, however, inference intervals fluctuate, meaning the temporal shift $\rho$ between chunks is a continuous real value (non-integer). Rounding this to integer steps causes timing mismatches and robot jitter. DASH decomposes the real-valued shift computed from precise arrival timestamps into integer step shifts and a fractional linear interpolation, carrying fractional remainders over to subsequent steps in an accumulative alignment algorithm. This delivers remarkably smooth trajectory control even under irregular asynchronous update cycles.

captions.F3: Process architecture and data flow in DASH. The environment, VLM (System 2), and action head (System 1) run on completely independent clocks, exchanging only the latest messages via LCM. Inside the action head, cached hidden features from the slow VLM are skillfully fused with fresh visual tokens captured by the fast ResNet.
captions.F4: Conceptual diagram of data sampling in desynchronized training. While standard training in (a) aligns all input timestamps, the proposed method in (b) intentionally retrieves the VLM input from an earlier frame $t-\Delta$, providing the action head with the latest frame $t$. This prepares the model for the time lags encountered during deployment.

sections.heading: Impressive reactivity validated on a real humanoid and in simulation
sections.summary: Across 50 RoboTwin tasks that incorporate inference latency into simulation time, DASH held 20 Hz even when scaling the VLM to 8B, substantially outperforming synchronous models in success rate. On a physical humanoid with dexterous five-finger hands, DASH also demonstrated a much higher task success rate over synchronous baselines.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Simulation evaluations were conducted in the RoboTwin bimanual environment. While standard simulators pause environment time during model inference, this study built an asynchronous simulation setup that charges the actual elapsed wall-clock inference time in simulation time, recreating the harsh constraints of reality. The benchmark comprises 50 diverse tasks (5 episodes each, 250 trials total) spanning pick-and-place, tool use, and in-hand reorientation. For physical validation, a humanoid robot with dexterous five-finger hands on both arms executed 24 language-instructed tabletop pick-and-place trials involving items like cans, chip bags, toy cars, and milk cartons.

### IV-B Simulation Evaluation: Latency-Agnostic Scaling
Benchmarked on an RTX 4090, standalone VLM inference latency grew from 53 ms (0.8B) to 193 ms (8B) as model size increased. In a conventional synchronous setup executing image preprocessing (15 ms) and action head inference (35 ms) serially, overall latency spanned 103 ms to 243 ms, cutting control frequency from 9.7 Hz down to 4.1 Hz. In contrast, DASH kept its critical path confined to the 50 ms preprocessing and action head run, holding a solid 20 Hz (a 2.1x to 4.9x speedup over synchronous control) across all sizes from 0.8B to 8B.

DASH also surpassed synchronous control in success rate (SR) across every model size (+1.0 to +5.9 percentage points), achieving a peak success rate of 69.5% with the 4B backbone. When desynchronized training was omitted (running asynchronous inference with standard training), the success rate dropped below the synchronous baseline, proving that pairing asynchronous execution with desynchronized training is essential.

### IV-C Real Humanoid Evaluation
In physical humanoid pick-and-place trials, standard synchronous execution with a fixed offset reached only 16/24 successes (66.7%), whereas DASH attained an outstanding 23/24 (95.8%). Under fixed offsets, subtle variations in inference intervals caused jitter at chunk boundaries, leading to grasping misalignments; DASH's adaptive temporal aggregator effectively eliminated this problem.

### IV-D Ablation Study: Backbone Freezing and Fresh Vision
Ablation experiments on the 4B model highlighted the critical role of the action head's standalone ResNet. Removing the in-head encoder while freezing the VLM caused the success rate to plummet to 55.0%. Fine-tuning the entire VLM backbone did not resolve the issue, reaching only 62.6%. The proposed DASH configuration (69.5%)—freezing the VLM to preserve web-scale representations while adding a trainable fresh vision encoder inside the action head—proved superior in both task performance and computational cost.

The robot smoothly executes complex tasks such as "pick up the cola with the left hand and place it in the white box" and "pick up the toy car with the right hand and place it in the white box" through dexterous five-finger hand control.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: Toward true real-time general-purpose robotics
sections.summary: By removing the VLM from the primary control loop, DASH successfully pairs the representational power of massive models with high-frequency 20 Hz control. While current evaluations focus on quasi-static tabletop manipulation, future work looks toward dynamic environments and full-body coordinated tasks.
sections.details:
This paper presented DASH, an asynchronous VLA system that decouples the VLM from the control loop to enable high-frequency control independent of model size. Combining cross-timescale fusion, desynchronized training, and adaptive temporal aggregation, DASH maintained a steady 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B up to 8B models, outperforming synchronous baselines in both simulation and real humanoid experiments.

The tasks evaluated in this study were primarily quasi-static manipulation. The authors anticipate that high reactivity and fresh visual perception will show their true value in dynamic settings with moving objects and long-horizon, dynamic whole-body control. Expanding evaluations into these more demanding, dynamic environments represents the natural next step.

takeaways: The assumption that larger VLA models inevitably slow down robots is a flaw of synchronous execution, which can be fully overcome by fast-slow asynchronous decoupling.
Contextual lag introduced by asynchronous separation is neatly solved by adding a dedicated fresh vision encoder to the action head and simulating time offsets during training.
Because inference intervals vary irregularly in asynchronous control, accumulative aggregation with fractional linear interpolation is essential for smoothly stitching action chunks.
Completely freezing the VLM backbone not only lowers compute costs but also improves success rates by clearly dividing roles between web-scale knowledge retention and manipulation adaptation.
limitations: Experimental evaluations focused on quasi-static tabletop pick-and-place tasks; verification in highly dynamic environments tracking fast-moving objects remains future work.
Because the VLM server and action server consume separate GPU resources and memory, edge compute requirements on the robot hardware are higher than in synchronous systems.

While the action head's ResNet compensates for low-level geometric changes, abrupt semantic scene changes (e.g., target objects suddenly hidden from view) cannot be reflected until the slower VLM update cycle completes.
